edition.deck: A close election in Brazil, a widening Starlink dispute and new pressure on UK and Danish politics.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritise live elections, security and consequential policy. Returning stories are included where today’s reporting adds a meaningful development or where the continuing stakes remain substantial.

content.headline: Brazil votes in a tight presidential runoff between Lula and Bolsonaro’s son
content.shortHeadline: Brazil votes in tight Lula-Bolsonaro runoff
content.standfirst: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is seeking another term against Flávio Bolsonaro, whose first-round lead surprised pollsters. Turnout could prove decisive, while the result may shape Brazil’s democratic direction.

image.caption: Flávio Bolsonaro and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva debate in São Paulo on 18 October.

sources.originalTitle: Brazilians vote in presidential election runoff pitting leftist Lula against far-right Bolsonaro
Fars dreng går efter den ultimative hævn i dag

segments.body: Brazilian voters are choosing between incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, in a runoff expected to be close. The final polls put Flávio slightly ahead, but the candidates entered election day virtually tied.

perspectives.body: DR’s account from Rio focuses on the Bolsonaro family’s political legacy and the enthusiasm of Flávio’s supporters there. Its reporting describes a campaign shaped by the prospect of Jair Bolsonaro’s return to influence if his son wins.

segments.title: A contested political legacy
segments.body: Flávio Bolsonaro has promised to pardon his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for attempting to overturn his 2022 defeat. Lula’s campaign has warned of the risks of a Bolsonaro return; supporters of Flávio argue the country needs change. The result is expected late Sunday.

content.headline: Ukraine says Starlink is stable as Musk confirms SpaceX imposed restrictions
content.shortHeadline: Starlink restored in Ukraine after SpaceX restrictions
content.standfirst: Ukraine says its connection is stable again, while Elon Musk says SpaceX restricted the service over alleged breaches of its terms. Kyiv disputes his account of how the network was used for drone strikes.

image.caption: A man in Kherson offers residents access to his Starlink internet after a Russian strike.

sources.originalTitle: Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored
Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?

segments.body: Ukrainian officials say Starlink connectivity has returned to normal after disruptions that Kyiv said hampered military operations. Elon Musk has now confirmed that SpaceX imposed restrictions, accusing Ukraine of using the civilian service for offensive drone strikes. Ukraine has disputed that claim; there was no immediate comment from its defence ministry.

segments.title: A reliance without a ready replacement
segments.body: Ukraine depends on Starlink for battlefield communications, but European alternatives cannot yet match its capabilities. The EU’s Govsatcom network is not currently suitable for drone warfare, while its planned Iris² system is not expected to be operational until 2029. Experts cited by the BBC say backups would improve resilience but would not replace Starlink’s full role.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s examination of alternatives finds no immediate equivalent to Starlink for Ukraine’s military needs. Govsatcom could provide a communications backup, but experts say it cannot currently support drone operations.

content.headline: Israel election nears amid West Bank crackdown and dispute over military service
content.shortHeadline: West Bank crackdown and draft row loom over Israel vote
content.standfirst: Israel plans to close West Bank crossings on election day as its operation in Hebron displaces residents. The election also turns on the exemption of ultra-Orthodox men from military service, a major point of tension in Netanyahu’s coalition.

image.caption: An Israeli army vehicle passes near the closed entrance to Hebron in the occupied West Bank.

sources.originalTitle: Israel to close West Bank crossings on election day as crackdown escalates
The bitter row over military service that could shape Israel's future
Tidligere militærgeneral udfordrer Netanyahu

segments.body: Israel’s military says all West Bank land crossings will close on Tuesday, barring Palestinian workers from entering. The move comes amid an operation in Hebron after two Israeli soldiers were killed in a shooting. Defence Minister Israel Katz said about 2,000 residents had been displaced; the military has demolished homes and businesses.

segments.title: A coalition under pressure
segments.body: The election is also being shaped by opposition to exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox men. The BBC reports that the exemption has become a key source of public anger as Israel fights wars on several fronts, and that Netanyahu needs the support of ultra-Orthodox parties to have a chance of staying in power. Recent polling cited by TV 2 puts the opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot’s party slightly ahead of Likud, but neither bloc appears likely to secure a majority.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s analysis describes the draft exemption as both a social fault line and a political risk for Netanyahu: his coalition depends on ultra-Orthodox parties, while opponents argue that the exemption is unfair as other Israelis serve.

content.headline: Serbia’s student movement challenges Vučić as turnout appears high
content.shortHeadline: High turnout could bolster Serbia’s student-led challenge
content.standfirst: Preliminary reports suggest record turnout in Serbia’s snap election, where a student-backed slate is trying to unseat long-serving leader Aleksandar Vučić. Results are still pending, and reports of irregularities and pressure on monitors have added to tensions.

image.caption: People queue outside a polling station in Novi Sad, Serbia’s second-largest city.

sources.originalTitle: Early reports suggest record high turnout in Serbia elections

segments.body: About 46% of eligible voters had cast ballots by 14:00 local time, nearly a million more than at the same point in the 2023 election, according to preliminary reports. The student-led Student List is challenging Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party after two years of protests sparked by a deadly railway-station collapse.

segments.title: A result under scrutiny
segments.body: The student slate is running on anti-corruption measures and changes to public media, while Vučić and his party deny corruption and media interference. There have been reports of attacks on election monitors and journalists, as well as videos alleging ballot irregularities. Voting was due to end at 20:00, with initial indications expected two hours later.

content.headline: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado returns from exile
content.shortHeadline: Machado returns to Venezuela after more than 10 months
content.standfirst: María Corina Machado says she is back in Venezuela after more than 10 months away. The political setting has changed sharply since she left, but the BBC’s initial report gives few details about her return or what she plans to do next.

sources.originalTitle: Venezuelan opposition leader María Machado returns after months in exile

segments.body: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado says she has returned to the country, writing on X: “I am here. With you.” Her ally, former presidential candidate Edmundo González Urrutia, confirmed that she was on Venezuelan soil.

Machado had left Venezuela to accept the Nobel Peace Prize in Norway. A month later, the United States seized President Nicolás Maduro; his deputy, Delcy Rodríguez, was sworn in as interim president and later signed an oil deal with the US. The BBC’s report is developing and does not yet explain the circumstances of Machado’s return.

content.headline: France protests continue as authorities report hundreds of thousands marching
content.shortHeadline: France protests continue; arrest totals differ by report
content.standfirst: The French interior ministry says 410,000 people protested on Saturday, while unions put the figure at twice that. Reports also differ on arrests: the interior minister told French media nearly 1,000 had been detained, while DR reported more than 1,300.

image.caption: Scenes from Saturday’s protests in France, where demonstrations included both peaceful marches and violent clashes.

sources.originalTitle: The images that show why Macron faces one of his biggest tests
Billeder: Brand i gaden og 'spejl' til politiet

segments.body: Demonstrations over the cost of living and public services continued across France. The interior ministry reported 410,000 participants nationwide and a 110,000-strong march in Paris; unions said the nationwide turnout was double the official figure. Police used tear gas and water cannon in several cities as clashes and vandalism were reported.

perspectives.body: DR reported more than 1,300 arrests, describing the figure as markedly lower than the previous weekend. The i Paper reported the interior minister saying nearly 1,000 people had been arrested, with the count expected to rise.

segments.title: A wider dispute over public services
segments.body: The protests began with student demonstrations over school conditions and staff shortages, then broadened to include living costs and opposition to the government. The interior minister said violence was less intense than the previous weekend, attributing the change to improved preparation. Further demonstrations have also taken place elsewhere in Europe.

content.headline: Salvadoran president says bodies found in Haiti are not the missing hostages
content.shortHeadline: Bukele says bodies found in Haiti are not Salvadoran hostages
content.standfirst: Nayib Bukele says four bodies handed to Salvadoran forces in Haiti are not those of the four missing technicians. Their identities remain uncertain as the search continues amid worsening gang violence.

image.caption: El Salvador’s president Nayib Bukele said the bodies handed to Salvadoran forces in Haiti were not the missing men.

sources.originalTitle: El Salvador president says bodies found in Haiti are not those of hostages

segments.body: El Salvador’s president says four bodies handed to his forces in Haiti are not those of the Salvadoran air technicians who disappeared last week. Bukele said one body was a child’s and another wore a uniform from a different country. The bodies have not been conclusively identified.

segments.title: A search amid gang violence
segments.body: The men were members of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force and were travelling in an armoured vehicle when they were ambushed in an area controlled by armed groups. Bukele has sent a military contingent to Haiti to recover them. The multinational force there has struggled to reach areas held by gangs.

content.headline: Gunmen kill at least 10 villagers in north-east Nigeria; toll may be higher
content.shortHeadline: At least 10 killed in village raid in north-east Nigeria
content.standfirst: Police say gunmen raided Binnari, looted shops and set homes alight. Witnesses and Amnesty International report higher possible death tolls, while police continue searching for people who may be missing or injured.

image.caption: File image of Nigerian police officers.

sources.originalTitle: Gunmen kill at least 10 villagers and loot shops in north-east Nigeria

segments.body: Police say gunmen on motorcycles attacked Binnari in Taraba state after midday prayers on Friday, killing at least 10 people, looting shops and setting houses ablaze. Officers are searching nearby bushland for people who may have been killed or wounded.

segments.title: The toll remains unclear
segments.body: Survivors told AFP they had counted at least 20 dead. Amnesty International’s Nigeria director said families reported up to 50 deaths, citing an initial funeral attended by 37 people. Police have confirmed 10 bodies so far and warned the death toll may rise.

content.headline: Storm Boelo leaves tens of thousands without power across northern UK
content.shortHeadline: Storm Boelo leaves 82,600 properties without power
content.standfirst: More than 82,000 properties remained without electricity on Sunday as strong winds disrupted rail and air travel across Scotland, Northern Ireland and northern England. Forecasters warn of further disruption and danger from flying debris and waves.

image.caption: Waves crash over the promenade during Storm Boelo in Largs, Scotland.

sources.originalTitle: More than 82,000 properties without power as Storm Boelo batters UK

segments.body: The Energy Networks Association said 82,600 properties were still without power on Sunday morning, including more than 30,000 in Scotland, after engineers restored service to 344,900 customers. The Met Office recorded gusts of up to 84mph in Argyll and Bute and warned of dangerous conditions in exposed areas.

segments.title: Travel and flooding disruption
segments.body: Flooding, fallen trees and speed restrictions disrupted rail services across Scotland, while flights were diverted or cancelled at Leeds Bradford airport. Flood warnings were active in parts of England and Scotland. The Met Office advised people in affected areas to secure loose items and stay indoors where possible.

content.headline: Burnham backs an evidence-based debate on possible EU free movement
content.shortHeadline: Burnham reopens debate on EU free movement
content.standfirst: The prime minister says options for closer ties with the EU should be discussed, including arrangements that could involve free movement. He says a fundamental change would need a mandate at a general election, expected by 2029.

image.caption: Andy Burnham said he believed the balance of migration had changed in recent years.

sources.originalTitle: Andy Burnham says he wants ‘honest discussion’ about freedom of movement with EU
Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement
Rayner backs Burnham call for debate on return to free movement with EU

segments.body: Andy Burnham has called for an “honest” and “evidence-based” debate about the UK’s future relationship with the EU, including the possibility of free movement. He has said any fundamental change would require a mandate at a general election. Burnham is due to meet EU leaders in Brussels on 20 November.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports that support for reopening the debate is not uniform within Labour: some ministers and MPs in pro-Brexit constituencies are wary, while cabinet minister Angela Rayner backs Burnham’s call as pragmatic.

segments.title: Trade-offs and political resistance
segments.body: Burnham has previously supported Labour’s 2024 manifesto, which ruled out returning to free movement, the single market or a customs union. Angela Rayner says the options should remain open, while Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch and Reform UK’s Robert Jenrick oppose the idea. Former chancellor Jeremy Hunt argues the UK should make the existing Brexit deal work.

segments.title: Migration figures have shifted
segments.body: The Guardian reports that net migration reached a record 944,000 in the year to March 2023 before falling to 171,000 last year, below the 2016 level. Burnham argues that the pattern of migration has changed since EU membership; critics warn that free movement could affect jobs and communities.

content.headline: Healey budget to give English mayors more borrowing and spending power
content.shortHeadline: Budget to give English mayors more borrowing power
content.standfirst: The planned devolution package includes a £1.5bn borrowing facility, £285m in initial growth funding and £150m to help councils manage larger budgets. The measures are due to be set out in Wednesday’s budget.

image.caption: Andy Burnham said the package would shift decisions from Westminster to local leaders.

sources.originalTitle: Healey’s first budget to include big devolution package to boost growth

segments.body: Chancellor John Healey is expected to announce a £1.5bn borrowing facility for English mayors and local leaders, developed with them over the next two years. The package also includes £285m in initial “good growth” funding next year, for local priorities such as housing, transport and high-street regeneration.

segments.title: Building local capacity
segments.body: A further £150m is planned to help councils administer larger budgets and build expertise. The funding is intended to bridge the period before a system due in 2028, under which some income-tax revenue would go directly to local areas. More details are expected in the budget.

content.headline: Tory candidate suspended after filmed claims about arranging contract killers
content.shortHeadline: Suspended Tory candidate faces investigation over hitman claims
content.standfirst: Jack Ross was suspended after an undercover Al Jazeera report showed him discussing violence and offering to broker contacts, according to the Guardian. Police in Scotland say they will review the programme; the allegations and party investigation remain unresolved.

image.caption: Jack Ross, a former Conservative local election candidate and Turning Point UK chief executive.

sources.originalTitle: Former Tory candidate suspended over contract killer claims was adviser in Kemi Badenoch’s office

segments.body: The Conservatives have suspended former candidate Jack Ross while investigating footage in which he appeared to discuss arranging violent acts for money. The Guardian reports that police in Scotland will review an Al Jazeera documentary showing Ross talking about using a far-right group and introducing a reporter to a man alleged to have links to the Ulster Volunteer Force.

segments.title: Questions over his party role
segments.body: The Guardian reports that Ross worked as a social media consultant in Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch’s office in 2025. Sources close to Badenoch described him as a junior external consultant; another party staffer told the paper that colleagues had raised concerns about his presence. Ross and Turning Point UK’s Nick Tenconi have been approached for comment.

content.headline: New analysis finds ethnic minorities less likely to get breast cancer via NHS
content.shortHeadline: Ethnic minorities less likely to get breast cancer screening diagnosis
content.standfirst: An analysis of more than 86,000 cases found people from Black, Asian and mixed backgrounds were up to a third less likely to be diagnosed through routine screening, and more likely to be diagnosed after an urgent referral or emergency presentation.

image.caption: People from several ethnic minority backgrounds were less likely to be diagnosed through routine breast screening, the analysis found.

sources.originalTitle: Ethnic minorities in England less likely to get breast cancer diagnosis from routine screening

segments.body: Researchers at the University of Surrey analysed 86,564 breast cancer diagnoses between 2009 and 2019. People from Black, Asian and mixed backgrounds, as well as those from deprived backgrounds, were up to 33% less likely to be diagnosed through routine screening and up to 37% more likely to be diagnosed in an emergency setting.

segments.title: Delays extend beyond screening
segments.body: The analysis also found people with learning disabilities waited 18% longer for diagnosis and 10% longer for treatment. Researchers say the findings point to inequalities in access to screening and timely care, though they do not establish every reason behind the differences.

content.headline: UK cocaine consumption has surged, with crime and health harms under scrutiny
content.shortHeadline: Cocaine use rises as linked crime and health harms mount
content.standfirst: Wastewater analysis suggests people in England consumed 123,000kg of cocaine in 2024–25, while police records mentioning the drug have risen. Researchers caution that the data cannot show how many individuals use cocaine or prove it caused a crime.

image.caption: Wastewater analysis estimates people in England consumed 123,000kg of cocaine in 2024–25.

sources.originalTitle: Cocaine-linked crimes on the rise in Britain as consumption surges
Ageing users and record deaths – the data behind Britain’s multibillion-pound cocaine habit
How cocaine conquered the UK: in pubs, festivals and workplaces the drug has become an everyday habit

segments.body: The Guardian’s investigation estimates cocaine consumption in England rose 26% from 2021 to 2024–25, reaching 123,000kg. Police forces that supplied data recorded a 10% rise in crimes mentioning cocaine since 2019. A mention in a police record does not establish that the drug caused an offence.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s analysis of the figures stresses that the wastewater estimate does not mean more people necessarily started using cocaine: a similar or smaller group may be taking it more often. The estimate also has substantial margins of error.

segments.title: More treatment and reported harms
segments.body: The Guardian reports that treatment starts for cocaine problems in England rose 57% between 2019–20 and 2024–25, with people in their 30s now the largest age group seeking help. Its crime analysis found that most recorded offences were drug offences, while 18% were violent crimes; experts caution that the figures do not prove the drug caused those crimes.

segments.title: Wider use in everyday settings
segments.body: Reporting from pubs, workplaces and festivals describes cocaine use becoming more visible and normalised as prices fell. Users and hospitality workers describe effects ranging from dependency to volatile behaviour. The Guardian’s reporting also notes that wastewater data cannot establish whether rising consumption reflects more users or more frequent use.

content.headline: Manchester’s Abu Dhabi property deals face renewed scrutiny over transparency
content.shortHeadline: Manchester’s Abu Dhabi property deals face scrutiny
content.standfirst: A Guardian investigation traces Abu Dhabi-linked investment in Manchester and raises questions about the terms, housing delivery and oversight of deals made by the council and regional authority. The council says it has received revenue and that reviews found the arrangements legal.

image.caption: Illustration of Sheikh Mansour’s Manchester property interests and Andy Burnham.

sources.originalTitle: ‘That’s the way the city works’: how the UAE changed the face of Andy Burnham’s Manchester

segments.body: A Guardian investigation says the UAE government and Emirati developers owned Manchester land and property equivalent to as much as 260 football pitches at its peak in 2023. It traces the investment to deals brokered after the UK government sought to maintain relations with the UAE, including a £1bn Manchester Life scheme.

segments.title: Housing and accountability questions
segments.body: Manchester Life promised more than 6,000 homes; the investigation says 2,039 have been delivered by the company, with another 2,839 built by other developers. It reports that only 8% of the 4,878 homes were classed as social or affordable, none provided by Manchester Life. The council says it received nearly £3m through profit-sharing and £17.6m in council tax.

segments.title: Deals under review
segments.body: Councillors are examining regional authority loans to property firms owned by Sheikh Mansour, which the authority says were repaid in full. A council review found weaknesses in documentation, monitoring and assurance around some deals. Former council leader Richard Leese defends the partnership as good for Manchester; critics question the cost and transparency of the arrangements.

content.headline: Meghan’s father denies allegations as Philippine authorities examine devices
content.shortHeadline: Thomas Markle denies allegations as Philippine inquiry continues
content.standfirst: Philippine authorities say they are examining digital material reportedly found at Thomas Markle Sr’s former home. Markle denies possessing child sexual abuse images; no findings have been released, and police say they will act if evidence supports charges.

image.caption: Thomas Markle Sr, pictured in a 2018 interview, has denied possessing child sexual abuse images.

sources.originalTitle: Signs suggest Thomas Markle Sr may be ‘sex offender of the grossest kind’, says Philippine minister

segments.body: Philippine authorities are examining digital material reportedly found at the former Cebu home of Thomas Markle Sr, the Duchess of Sussex’s estranged father. Interior minister Jonvic Remulla told the Guardian that forensic work is continuing and that officials want to establish the contents before releasing findings.

segments.title: Claims and denials
segments.body: Markle Sr denies possessing child sexual abuse images and says the devices were not in his possession after he left the Philippines. His son reported finding the material, according to the Guardian. Philippine police say they will coordinate with other authorities and take legal action if there is sufficient evidence to charge him.

segments.title: UK police review
segments.body: The Metropolitan Police confirmed it passed a 2019 letter containing claims of alleged offending outside the UK to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, but did not share details with other law-enforcement agencies. The force is considering whether to refer its handling to the Independent Office for Police Conduct. The allegations remain under investigation.

content.headline: Venstre faces internal pressure over pesticide ban and farm compensation
content.shortHeadline: Venstre members demand full compensation over pesticide ban
content.standfirst: A TV 2 survey of party members with elected or organisational roles found many oppose backing a national pesticide ban unless all affected landowners are compensated. Some put the cost at 20bn–30bn kroner, intensifying pressure on party leader Troels Lund Poulsen.

image.caption: Søren Gade and Troels Lund Poulsen at a meeting in the Danish parliament.

source.credit: Foto: Mads Claus Rasmussen / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Dele af Troels Lunds bagland stiller ultimatum og kræver tocifret milliarderstatning
ANALYSE: Derfor er dagens møde så vigtigt for Troels Lund – og hvad kan gå helt galt eller godt?
Troels Lund burde 'stramme bardunerne', mener Venstrekoryfæ

segments.body: More than 240 of 943 Venstre members with party roles responded to TV 2’s survey. Among those opposed to backing a national pesticide ban without compensation for everyone affected, several demanded full compensation and cited a total of 20bn–30bn kroner. These are respondents’ demands, not an agreed compensation plan.

segments.title: Leadership faces a test
segments.body: The dispute follows a split over the fertiliser law and Søren Gade’s departure from parliament. Venstre’s extraordinary executive-board meeting is a test of whether party leader Troels Lund Poulsen can maintain support for the party’s green direction while members seek guarantees for farmers. The party leadership says Venstre supports a national ban and wants affected people treated fairly.

perspectives.body: TV 2’s survey shows the party’s rural base is not uniformly behind the leadership: some respondents say they will not support a pesticide ban without full compensation, while others back a greener profile with safeguards for farmers.

content.headline: Inger Støjberg says Danmarksdemokraterne must appeal beyond rural voters
content.shortHeadline: Støjberg shifts Danmarksdemokraterne’s focus beyond rural voters
content.standfirst: After criticism of the party’s weak election performance and narrow focus, Inger Støjberg says it should appeal to suburban voters as well as people in the countryside. Members raised concerns about its visibility and attention to issues beyond farming and rural life.

image.caption: Inger Støjberg speaks to the press after her party’s annual meeting in Herning.

source.credit: Foto: Mikkel Berg Pedersen / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Det begynder at knage i Støjbergs bagland: - Vi har lavet mange fodfejl, og det har Inger også fået at vide

segments.body: Danmarksdemokraterne leader Inger Støjberg announced a change of emphasis at the party’s annual meeting: it should speak not only to voters by the country road but also to those living behind suburban hedges. The move follows poor election results and weak polling, and criticism from members of the party’s organisational base.

segments.title: Members want a broader agenda
segments.body: Party members told TV 2 that Danmarksdemokraterne had focused too heavily on issues such as wolves, solar farms and farming, while giving too little attention to elderly care and eastern Denmark. Local figures said Støjberg had listened to criticism of the campaign and her visibility. She said the party could use more political energy and variety.

content.headline: Copenhagen Metro stations cannot serve as shelters without major changes
content.shortHeadline: Copenhagen Metro needs rebuilding to serve as a shelter
content.standfirst: Emails seen by DR say skylights, ventilation and toilet facilities make the city’s underground stations unsuitable as public shelters in their current form. The Metro company says it is preparing a few spaces for short-term protection of a limited number of passengers.

sources.originalTitle: Københavnsk metro kan ikke være beskyttelsesrum uden ombygning

segments.body: Copenhagen’s Metro cannot be used as a public shelter in its current form, according to emails between Metro company officials and Copenhagen Municipality obtained by DR. Skylights could shatter, while ventilation and toilet facilities are also obstacles to using stations for protection during an attack.

segments.title: Limited preparations underway
segments.body: The company says it is preparing some spaces for short-term protection of a limited number of passengers already in the Metro. The work is not the same as converting stations into public shelters. The correspondence also identifies Metro bicycle basements as a possible option.

content.headline: Orø residents plan backup radios and power for an emergency
content.shortHeadline: Orø prepares backup communications for emergencies
content.standfirst: The island’s volunteer response group plans to use UHF radios to contact local first responders if power or mobile networks fail. Holbæk Municipality has also promised backup power for a community hall linked to the clinic and care centre.

image.caption: Signe Olsen is part of Orø’s volunteer emergency preparedness group.

sources.originalTitle: Ø ruster sig til at blive afskåret fra omverdenen med UHF-radioer og nødstrøm

segments.body: Orø residents are planning a local communications network for emergencies, when a loss of power or mobile service could delay help reaching the island. Volunteers want to use UHF radios to connect the community hall with local first responders and, through a link to the mainland, the emergency call centre.

segments.title: A local response point
segments.body: The community hall is intended to serve as the island’s information point, with a fire engine stationed there and a SINE radio link to call 112. Holbæk Municipality has promised backup power for the hall, which is connected to the medical clinic and care centre. The island has also distributed an emergency guide to households.

content.headline: Digital tools help some residents with dementia reconnect with memories
content.shortHeadline: Memory technology helps some residents with dementia reconnect
content.standfirst: A Danish Health Authority review of 15 pilot projects found that tools including personal photo cubes, digital frames and virtual reality can support wellbeing and help relatives and care staff connect with people with dementia.

image.caption: Trien Ly shows his father a Memory Cube displaying personal photos and videos.

sources.originalTitle: 'Nærmest mirakuløst': Dement far genkendte julesweater - nu vil han ikke gå i andet

segments.body: A Danish Health Authority review of 15 pilot projects found that digital tools can help some people with dementia engage with family and care staff. At Ceres Centre in Horsens, a Memory Cube displays family-selected photos and videos; one resident recognised an old Christmas sweater in a picture and wanted to keep wearing one like it.

segments.title: Support for daily care
segments.body: Care staff in the review described using familiar images to calm a resident during morning care, avoiding medication or physical intervention in that instance. The authority says the tools may support wellbeing and make care easier, but the report describes pilot projects rather than proving the same effect for everyone.

content.headline: Extra school-nurse conversations cut absence for three in four pupils in pilot
content.shortHeadline: School-nurse pilot reduced absence for three in four pupils
content.standfirst: At Nørrebro Park School, three in four of 32 pupils in the programme’s first two years reduced their absence. The approach is now being extended to 13 other Copenhagen schools, though the school’s head says some pupils later return to old patterns.

image.caption: School nurse Helle Attrup-Christiansen helped start the programme to reduce pupil absence.

sources.originalTitle: Hun talte gang på gang med børn, der havde det ”fint” – men deres fravær fortalte en anden historie

segments.body: Nørrebro Park School began offering extra conversations with a school nurse to fifth-graders with more than five periods of absence in six months. In the first two years, three in four of the 32 participating pupils reduced their absence. Copenhagen is now expanding the programme to 13 other primary schools.

segments.title: Looking beyond the classroom
segments.body: The nurse asks about pupils’ physical and mental health, school life and home circumstances, then works with families and the school to identify what may help. One pupil worried about a seriously ill parent was given a watch so he could check in. The school’s head says some children fall back into earlier absence patterns if the school does not follow up.

content.headline: Danish dairies sell milk produced using cow-and-calf methods
content.shortHeadline: New Danish milk products keep calves with their mothers longer
content.standfirst: Two dairies are selling milk from farms where calves can drink from their mothers or a foster cow for their first three months. The products remain niche, and experts say higher prices can limit consumer demand.

sources.originalTitle: En ny type mælk har fundet vej til køledisken

segments.body: Øllingegaard and Thise dairies sell milk produced using a cow-and-calf approach: calves have priority to drink from their mother or a foster cow for their first three months, with surplus milk sold to consumers. Thise launched its product in 2019; Øllingegaard introduced its version in March 2026.

segments.title: A niche market
segments.body: The dairies report growing interest from some farmers and customers, but a food-culture expert says the products still appeal to a small group. Price remains decisive for many shoppers, and the expert says wider change may require regulation or shared industry standards rather than consumer choice alone.

content.headline: Researchers challenge food lobby’s use of forest nitrogen figures
content.shortHeadline: Researchers dispute food lobby’s claims about nitrogen from forests
content.standfirst: Two researchers say unusually high readings from a handful of forests do not show that forests generally release more nitrogen than farmland. Fødevaredanmark says it wants those readings investigated and continues to call for a pause to regulation.

image.caption: Forests can absorb air pollution, including ammonia from nearby farms, which can later enter the soil as nitrogen.

source.credit: Foto: Bo Amstrup / Bo Amstrup / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Lobbyorganisation råbte op om skove – forskere kalder det "vrøvl"

segments.body: Fødevaredanmark cited five forests with high nitrogen readings in arguing that the basis for agricultural nitrogen regulation should be reviewed. Two researchers told TV 2 that the examples cannot be used to describe forests generally, and that much of the nitrogen in those forests may originate from nearby farms.

segments.title: Different readings of the evidence
segments.body: The researchers say forests generally release far less nitrogen than farmland and can absorb pollution from surrounding agriculture. Fødevaredanmark says it did not claim that all forests are representative and wants high readings, including in old or unmanaged woodland, examined further. The organisation still supports pausing the regulation.

perspectives.body: Fødevaredanmark says its point is that some forest areas have unusually high nitrogen concentrations, not that all forests behave alike. It argues those cases warrant further investigation before the regulation proceeds.

content.headline: Jack Antonoff on grief, his breakup and refusing to rewrite the past
content.shortHeadline: Jack Antonoff on singing through a breakup
content.standfirst: The Bleachers frontman says he will keep performing songs written about his marriage, even after its end. He also discusses survivor’s guilt, his work as a producer and speaking out on politics and ticket prices.

image.caption: Jack Antonoff (second from right) with Bleachers.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I’d rather live through something publicly than escape it privately’: Jack Antonoff on survivor’s guilt and still singing love songs after his breakup

segments.body: Jack Antonoff says he considered changing Bleachers’ setlist after his marriage ended, but decided the songs belonged in the show. He sees that decision as part of an agreement with his audience: to sing honestly about how he felt, and to stand by those feelings when life changes.

segments.title: A public voice
segments.body: Antonoff says his drive is tied, in part, to survivor’s guilt following his younger sister’s death. He also rejects the idea that he writes songs and hands them to pop stars, and speaks bluntly about ticket prices and his support for Palestine.

content.headline: Clubbers debate whether talking, phones and drugs are killing the dancefloor
content.shortHeadline: What belongs on the dancefloor?
content.standfirst: A plea for quieter crowds has reopened an argument about club etiquette. DJs and dancers disagree over whether conversation builds community or breaks the spell, amid concerns about phone use, drug trends and the cost of going out.

image.caption: A crowd dancing at Manchester’s Hacienda in 1989.

sources.originalTitle: Murder on the dancefloor: are phones, drugs and chatter killing off dancing?

segments.body: DJ Jane Fitz’s request for people to stop chatting through sets struck a nerve across clubland. Some welcomed the appeal; others argued that paying to get in should mean being free to talk. For DJ James Ronald, conversation is part of how people connect, while historian Dan Beaumont says clubs need both talkers and dancers.

segments.title: The changing club
segments.body: DJs and venue workers also point to phone filming, crowded rooms, quieter sound levels and rising costs as pressures on dancefloors. Some venues now restrict phones, while one London space uses separate directions for dancing and chatting. Fitz says she has already noticed people listening more during quieter moments in sets.

content.headline: Raye’s Mercury prize win celebrates a bold album—and raises questions
content.shortHeadline: Raye wins the Mercury for a 73-minute album
content.standfirst: Raye won the 2026 Mercury prize for This Music May Contain Hope, a genre-spanning record that puts the album form ahead of streaming-era brevity. The award’s increasingly commercial shortlist has also prompted questions about its purpose.

image.caption: Raye accepts the 2026 Mercury prize.

sources.originalTitle: Raye wins 2026 Mercury prize for This Music May Contain Hope

segments.body: Raye’s second studio album, This Music May Contain Hope, won the 2026 Mercury prize in Newcastle. The 73-minute record ranges across big-band jazz, funk and power ballads; its hit single, “Where Is My Husband!”, reached No 1 in the UK. Raye said she was grateful to have an album recognised after years of feeling pushed towards singles.

segments.title: The prize’s direction
segments.body: The win came amid concern that the Mercury shortlist is becoming more commercially successful and less distinct from the Brit awards. Six shortlisted albums reached No 1, and most were released by or alongside major labels. Paul McCartney and Suede were among those who missed out.

content.headline: Taylor Swift’s early Myspace fans remember the years before fame
content.shortHeadline: Taylor Swift’s Myspace-era fans look back
content.standfirst: A teenage fan recalls following Swift online before her 2006 debut album made her a star. The essay traces how early social media turned fandom into a shared project—and how Swift’s success changed the meaning of being a fan.

image.caption: Taylor Swift in her early career as a teenage country singer.

sources.originalTitle: The Taylor Swift I knew on Myspace in 2006

segments.body: Before Taylor Swift was famous in the UK, fans found her on Myspace and gathered small scraps of information about her life and music. One teenager recalls writing on Swift’s page, collecting press clippings and sharing the excitement with friends who felt the young singer understood them.

segments.title: A fan community grows up
segments.body: The writer remembers Swift’s debut as a tender collection of songs about teenage romance and uncertainty. Looking back, she sees the community as part of the experience: fans helped one another discover the music and treated the singer’s early success as something they had witnessed together.

content.headline: Fontaines DC’s rise began with ambition in Dublin’s small venues
content.shortHeadline: Fontaines DC: from Dublin student band to stadiums
content.standfirst: Early teachers, promoters and fans recall the group’s rapid development from college rehearsals and small Dublin gigs to major stages. Their ambition was apparent early, though the band’s story also includes the loss of a key supporter.

image.caption: Grian Chatten and Conor Deegan III performing with Fontaines DC.

sources.originalTitle: The breathtaking rise of Fontaines DC, by the people who were there

segments.body: Fontaines DC formed at the Dublin campus of BIMM and quickly stood out to people around them. The college’s dean recalls a band that kept adding new songs and made clear plans for where it wanted to go. Early audiences saw a distinctive group, even before its members were playing headline shows.

segments.title: The people around the band
segments.body: The account follows the group from local support slots to international recognition, drawing on memories from a college dean, an early promoter and a publican who booked them. The article also remembers promoter Trevor Dietz, who helped build their early shows and died before the band’s planned stadium dates.

content.headline: Ne-Yo’s debut made tenderness a route to R&B stardom
content.shortHeadline: How Ne-Yo made heartfelt R&B his calling card
content.standfirst: A 20th-anniversary reassessment finds In My Own Words at its strongest when Ne-Yo turns lived relationship details into polished pop-R&B. The review also places his gentle approach against a genre shifting toward harder-edged hip-hop.

sources.originalTitle: In My Own Words

segments.body: Ne-Yo’s 2006 debut arrived amid competition from younger R&B stars, but made a case for songwriting as a path to solo success. In My Own Words pairs his light tenor with streamlined production and songs that treat care, heartbreak and courtesy as material for confident pop.

segments.title: A songwriter’s point of view
segments.body: The review traces how Ne-Yo drew on stories from women in his family and circle, shaping material that he said was often based on real events. It praises the album’s emotional specificity while noting that his polished, considerate style differed from the more forceful direction mainstream R&B was taking.

content.headline: Beirut City Pop gathers music made amid Lebanon’s civil war
content.shortHeadline: The music Beirut made through civil war
content.standfirst: Habibi Funk’s compilation collects Lebanese soul, disco and jazz from the late 1970s and early 1980s. The review hears music shaped by outside influences and local solidarity, while questioning whether “city pop” is the right frame.

sources.originalTitle: Beirut City Pop

segments.body: Beirut City Pop gathers recordings made during Lebanon’s civil war, when musicians worked in a close-knit scene and shared music through copied tapes. The compilation highlights artists who turned to soul, disco and jazz amid a conflict that had a profound effect on everyday life.

segments.title: A name with limits
segments.body: The review questions the compilation’s “city pop” framing: Beirut’s private-press music may share some surface features with Japanese city pop, but it came from a different musical and social world. One song’s lyrics about daily car bombs bring the violence into direct focus.

content.headline: Eris Drew and Octo Octa turn dance-music history into a joyful album
content.shortHeadline: Eris Drew and Octo Octa make dance music for fun
content.standfirst: The collaborators built their first full-length together in a New Hampshire cabin, drawing on vintage dance records, samples and live instruments. The review celebrates the album’s maximalist playfulness and a more intimate song at its centre.

sources.originalTitle: Alchemical Sisters

segments.body: For Alchemical Sisters, Eris Drew and Octo Octa made a studio in their New Hampshire cabin and assembled a maximalist record from synthesizers, psych-folk instruments and samples from their dance-music archive. The sound recalls 1990s big beat, with tracks that value exuberance over the dancefloor’s usual function.

segments.title: A personal centre
segments.body: The album moves through high-energy references and shifting rhythms, but the review singles out “Song for New Hampshire” as its warmest moment. The track turns the duo’s shared life and chosen family into a sincere, gently idealistic song.

content.headline: Ali G recruit says he recognised Sacha Baron Cohen and played along
content.shortHeadline: Ali G recruit says he knew the joke
content.standfirst: Joshua Loudermilk says he suspected Sacha Baron Cohen was behind the character Col Erran Morad, but stayed in character and tried to out-improvise him. That account differs from the film’s repeated claim that its recruits were unaware of the joke.

image.caption: Joshua Loudermilk in the trailer for Ali G: Who Iz I?

sources.originalTitle: Ali G: Who Iz I? stooge says he was in on joke but didn’t tell Sacha Baron Cohen: ‘He’s not going to punk me. I’ll trick him’

segments.body: Joshua Loudermilk says he worked out that the Israeli commander recruiting him for Ali G: Who Iz I? was Sacha Baron Cohen, but decided not to break character. He says he welcomed the chance to improvise, and treated the shoot as an opportunity to test his comedy acting.

segments.title: A disputed account
segments.body: The film presents Loudermilk and fellow recruit Michael Aboud as unaware of the prank. Loudermilk says he posted publicly about filming with Cohen soon after the shoot, but the production did not see the posts. The Guardian reports that the film’s representatives again said Loudermilk was not in on the joke and had not yet answered a follow-up question.

content.headline: Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love asks who has the right to tell a worker’s story
content.shortHeadline: Lee Chang-dong on class, work and Possible Love
content.standfirst: The director’s new film follows a working-class couple facing redundancy and a wealthy filmmaker who wants to document their lives. Lee says the story is also about the power imbalance between a camera-holder and their subject.

image.caption: Director Lee Chang-dong.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Fighting an impossible fight is the only way to reclaim dignity’: Lee Chang-dong on class warfare and his searing Oscar contender

segments.body: Possible Love grew from the 2009 Ssangyong Motors strike, when workers occupied a factory to protest planned layoffs. Lee Chang-dong says he hesitated over whether he was worthy of telling a story about the workers’ suffering, and how close a filmmaker should stand to their subjects.

segments.title: The power of looking
segments.body: The film places a documentary filmmaker’s camera between two couples with sharply different access to wealth. Lee says the person behind the camera has power even without intending to use it. He sees telling stories about people pushed to society’s margins as a moral responsibility, and describes their struggle as a way to reclaim dignity.

content.headline: A documentary follows Teesside fishers seeking answers after a mass die-off
content.shortHeadline: Teesside fishers keep seeking answers about the die-off
content.standfirst: Jeanie Finlay’s film follows fisher Stan Rennie and others campaigning after thousands of crustaceans died along the north-east coast in 2021. The cause remains unresolved, while the fishers are raising money for further scientific testing.

image.caption: Fisher Stan Rennie in his boat in Hartlepool.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Overnight, everything was dead’: the Teesside fisherman turned activist dubbed the Mr Bates of the seas

segments.body: After a mass die-off of crabs and lobsters in 2021, Teesside fisher Stan Rennie joined a campaign to understand what had happened. Jeanie Finlay’s documentary follows Rennie over four years; she says the film cannot provide an official cause, but can show what the search for answers has meant to those affected.

segments.title: An unresolved dispute
segments.body: Authorities have denied a link between the die-off and dredging near the Tees, attributing it to an algae bloom and later a pathogen. Fishers and local campaigners dispute those explanations. The documentary follows their efforts, including fundraising for more scientific tests; the mayor has rejected claims of wrongdoing.

content.headline: Wildwood brings Laika’s handcrafted stop-motion to a new forest adventure
content.shortHeadline: Wildwood offers old-fashioned stop-motion adventure
content.standfirst: Laika’s new family film sends two children into a hidden world of talking animals and strange creatures. The review praises its tactile animation and exuberant storytelling, while finding its central threat less compelling than the opening.

image.caption: Prue, voiced by Peyton Elizabeth Lee, in Wildwood.

sources.originalTitle: Wildwood review – Laika’s pleasingly old fashioned stop-motion magic-forest odyssey

segments.body: When crows carry off her baby brother, 12-year-old Prue and her classmate Curtis follow them into a forest beside Portland, Oregon. There they find an unfamiliar world of talking animals, oppressed people and a dangerous governess. The film adapts the book by Carson Ellis and Colin Meloy in Laika’s stop-motion style.

segments.title: A tactile fantasy
segments.body: The review welcomes the physical immediacy of Laika’s animation and the film’s good-natured, old-fashioned sense of adventure. It is less convinced by the clarity of the governess’s motive and says the story lacks the sustained scare of Coraline, though its opening has an uncanny edge.

content.headline: The Social Reckoning review: a chilling film about Facebook’s power
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning turns Facebook’s record into horror
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to The Social Network dramatises the reporting around Facebook’s internal documents and whistleblower Frances Haugen. Its reviewer finds the film frightening partly because the revelations have become so familiar.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: I was terrified watching The Social Reckoning – then went back to scrolling

segments.body: The Social Reckoning follows journalist Jeff Horwitz and former Facebook employee Frances Haugen as she shares internal information about the company’s algorithms, teen mental health and political misinformation. The film moves between their reporting and Mark Zuckerberg’s preparations for a Senate hearing.

segments.title: The unsettling aftermath
segments.body: The review describes the film as an investigative drama that turns into a horror story about social media’s place in everyday life. Its writer says the revelations left her disturbed, but also reflects that she still relies on Meta’s products—an unresolved dependence that makes the film’s warning personal.

content.headline: November films to watch: from Elsinore to The Hunger Games
content.shortHeadline: What to watch in November: 12 film picks
content.standfirst: A month-ahead guide ranges from Andrew Scott as actor Ian Charleson to a new Hunger Games prequel, with dramas, comedy and animation among the releases. Dates and availability vary by country.

sources.originalTitle: Elsinore to The Hunger Games: 12 of the best films to watch in November

segments.body: The November selection includes Elsinore, with Andrew Scott playing actor Ian Charleson in the final months of his life, and Sunrise on the Reaping, a new Hunger Games prequel. It also highlights Club Kid, about a New York party promoter who discovers he has a son, and Disney animation Hexed.

segments.title: More to look out for
segments.body: The guide also picks out films about the making of Rocky, disability-rights activist Judith Heumann, and a care-home manager whose friendship with a visiting theatre director grows over time. It supplies release dates across cinemas and streaming services in several territories.

content.headline: You Can See Everything leaves Elizabeth Holmes’s claims unresolved
content.shortHeadline: A documentary meets Elizabeth Holmes before prison
content.standfirst: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim filmed the Theranos founder shortly before she reported to prison. Their documentary gives her room to tell her version of events, then complicates the encounter without settling whether she is manipulative or deluded.

sources.originalTitle: 'As famous and defiant as ever': Why Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes remains the US's most fascinating fraudster

segments.body: You Can See Everything follows Elizabeth Holmes, her partner and their children in the weeks before she went to prison for defrauding investors. Holmes says she did not lie and that her blood-testing device worked; the film presents her account alongside the filmmakers’ visible scepticism.

segments.title: A question of interpretation
segments.body: The documentary changes direction when Fielder brings another person into the conversation, raising the possibility that he, too, might be drawn into Holmes’s story. The film does not decide whether she is deliberately manipulative or believes her own claims, leaving that uncertainty at its centre.

content.headline: La Bola Negra’s century-spanning story of gay lives heads to UK cinemas
content.shortHeadline: La Bola Negra connects three gay lives across time
content.standfirst: Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s film links three men’s stories across a century of Spanish history. Its festival reception and awards attention have raised expectations, though its UK cinema release is still ahead.

sources.originalTitle: 'Immediately spellbinding': Four reasons why gay Spanish epic La Bola Negra could win the Oscar for best picture

segments.body: La Bola Negra follows three gay men in 1932, 1937 and 2017, connecting stories of desire, rejection and historical memory. The film draws on the work of Federico García Lorca and moves between romance, historical drama and family history.

segments.title: Festival momentum
segments.body: The film won a major audience award in Toronto after earlier festival attention, and its reception has fuelled Oscar speculation. The article points to its visual ambition and performances, while reporting that UK cinemas are due to release it on 6 November.

content.headline: Larry David’s biographer won him over with baseball, not questions
content.shortHeadline: How Larry David’s reluctant biography came together
content.standfirst: Blake J Harris recounts how the Seinfeld and Curb Your Enthusiasm creator resisted an authorised biography, then agreed to take part. The book traces how David’s unruly life fed into his comedy.

image.caption: Larry David, subject of the new biography.

sources.originalTitle: ‘There’s nothing interesting about me – and no interest in me’: how Larry David’s new biography nearly didn’t happen

segments.body: Larry David initially told biographer Blake J Harris that there was little reason to write about him. Harris persisted, with help from David’s friends and collaborator Jeff Schaffer. At their first meeting, Harris chose to talk about the New York Yankees rather than immediately question David about his career.

segments.title: Life becomes material
segments.body: Harris’s account links David’s early experiences—including quitting Saturday Night Live and laughing at a Pez dispenser during a recital—to episodes of Seinfeld and Curb Your Enthusiasm. The biography also describes the long stretch when David struggled for work before his television success.

content.headline: Seven shows to stream this week, from Nocturne to Matthew Perry
content.shortHeadline: What to stream this week: Nocturne and more
content.standfirst: The week’s picks include a claustrophobic crime thriller led by Stephen Graham and an intimate series about Matthew Perry. The selection also ranges across comedy, competition and returning drama.

image.caption: Stephen Graham in Nocturne.

sources.originalTitle: Nocturne to The One About Matthew Perry: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: Nocturne leads the selection: Stephen Graham plays a prisoner whose apparent alibi does not stop police suspecting his involvement in a missing-child case. Another pick is a three-part series about Matthew Perry, combining interviews with friends and family and reflections on his career and struggles.

segments.title: More to watch
segments.body: Other choices include the Channel 4 phone-first drama The Guest List, Netflix comedy Minimum Wage and a darts contest featuring Luke Littler. The guide also covers new instalments of Dexter and American Horror Story, with platform and release details for each.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors’ turret is missing risk and spontaneity
content.shortHeadline: Why this year’s Celebrity Traitors turret feels flat
content.standfirst: A review of the latest episode argues that the show’s remaining Traitors are either too cautious or too polished. Kenny’s arrival has brought energy, but James Acaster’s reluctance to take risks is testing the format.

image.caption: Maya Jama and Richard E Grant induct James Acaster into the Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Claudia picked the wrong Traitors

segments.body: The review argues that this series has repeatedly chosen the wrong Traitors: Richard E Grant revealed himself early, Hannah Fry faced suspicion quickly, and James Acaster has struggled to embrace the role. In the latest mission, his refusal to take part helped leave the team with no prize money.

segments.title: A needed change of pace
segments.body: The writer finds Maya Jama’s polished game-play less entertaining than the awkwardness and risk that make the format compelling. Kenny, the newest recruit, is the exception: his shock at being chosen brought a burst of mischief to the turret.

content.headline: Eleven overlooked detective series to find on BBC iPlayer
content.shortHeadline: Eleven detective shows to discover on BBC iPlayer
content.standfirst: This guide ranges from village mysteries and comic crime drama to cold-case investigations and rural noir. It is designed for viewers who have exhausted the familiar British detective favourites.

sources.originalTitle: The 11 most-underrated detective series to watch on BBC iPlayer

segments.body: The recommendations include The Hairdresser Mysteries, a new daytime whodunnit starring Sally Phillips, and Istanbul-set detective drama The Turkish Detective. The guide also singles out The Jetty, with Jenna Coleman as a police officer investigating a case close to home.

segments.title: Beyond the familiar
segments.body: Other picks include the Scottish comic series Hamish Macbeth, Australian rural noir High Country and the cold-case team drama Waking the Dead. The selection also covers Annika, Dalziel and Pascoe and a newer Death in Paradise spin-off.

content.headline: James Acaster’s Celebrity Traitors style has viewers taking notice
content.shortHeadline: Why James Acaster has become a Traitors crush
content.standfirst: An essay argues that Acaster’s carefully chosen clothes, nervousness and reluctant Traitor role have made him an unexpected object of affection for viewers. The appeal, it suggests, is the contrast between competence and vulnerability.

image.caption: James Acaster on The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Why women love James Acaster

segments.body: The article reads the audience’s interest in James Acaster through the contrast between his public comic persona and his measured presence on The Celebrity Traitors. His clothes—chore jackets, well-cut trousers and simple T-shirts—also stand out against the show’s more flamboyant styling.

segments.title: The appeal of reluctance
segments.body: Acaster was recruited as a Traitor against his will, and the essay sees his unease about lying as part of his appeal. It frames the audience response as projection rather than simply a verdict on his looks: viewers are drawn to the combination of awkwardness, style and apparent sincerity.

content.headline: Isy Suttie on Taskmaster, Peep Show and making room for creativity
content.shortHeadline: Isy Suttie on Taskmaster and life after Peep Show
content.standfirst: The comedian and actor says Taskmaster has revived a willingness to trust her instincts. She also reflects on Peep Show’s enduring comfort for viewers and how parenthood has changed her songwriting.

image.caption: Isy Suttie, who is appearing on Taskmaster.

sources.originalTitle: Peep Show’s Isy Suttie: ‘I muted a part of myself since having kids’

segments.body: Isy Suttie says the uncertainty of Taskmaster has brought back a part of herself that had become quieter since having children and getting older. The comedian, actor and writer has moved between stand-up, radio, books and screen roles, including Dobby in Peep Show.

segments.title: The work that stays
segments.body: Suttie says Peep Show fans have told her the series helped them through difficult periods, a feeling she understands from her own attachment to The Inbetweeners during grief. She also says she has found it harder to write songs since becoming a parent, though she is still making new work.

content.headline: Strictly Come Dancing’s themed weeks are distracting from the dancing
content.shortHeadline: Strictly should give its fancy-dress weeks a rest
content.standfirst: This year’s early themed shows have left half the celebrities dancing in costume, an opinion piece argues. The writer enjoys Strictly’s spectacle but says extra dress-up, sketches and presenters risk crowding out the contestants’ progress.

image.caption: Dianne Buswell and Will Best perform during Strictly’s Icons Week.

sources.originalTitle: Strictly needs to calm down – and give the fancy-dress themed weeks a rest

segments.body: The article argues that Strictly’s early Movies and Icons weeks have made themed dressing too frequent. Costumes and character impressions, it says, can distract from the show’s central appeal: celebrities learning to dance and becoming more confident over time.

segments.title: Let the journey unfold
segments.body: The writer is not calling for a purist ballroom competition and enjoys the show’s theatrical side, especially Halloween week. The concern is that extra presenters, sketches and novelty themes suggest a lack of confidence in the contestants’ development, which becomes more compelling as the series progresses.

content.headline: What to watch on TV tonight: Adultery and This City Is Ours return
content.shortHeadline: Tonight on TV: Adultery and This City Is Ours
content.standfirst: The evening guide highlights a new drama about an affair and the return of Liverpool-set gang series This City Is Ours. It also includes architecture, fishing and a Bill Murray travelogue.

image.caption: Romola Garai and Dominic Cooper in Adultery.

sources.originalTitle: TV tonight: a horny drama stuffed with sex in a car, toilet and … city farm

segments.body: Adultery begins with personal trainer Beth, played by Romola Garai, drawn to doctor Tom, played by Dominic Cooper, after a death in her social circle. The six-part drama follows their affair and its consequences. This City Is Ours returns with its Liverpool gang story, as trouble finds Michael and Diana in Spain.

segments.title: More in the evening line-up
segments.body: Kevin McCloud examines which buildings are preserved and why, while Bill Murray appears in a travelogue following a golf tour of Ireland. The listings also flag new episodes of fishing and reality programmes, with channel and start-time information.

content.headline: BioWare’s closure leaves Mass Effect fans mourning a lost future
content.shortHeadline: BioWare’s closure leaves Mass Effect fans bereft
content.standfirst: A former fan and games-industry worker reflects on EA’s reported studio closure, cancelled Mass Effect plans and the loss of more than 400 jobs. The piece also explains why the original trilogy’s choices and characters remain so powerful.

image.caption: Mass Effect 3, part of BioWare’s original trilogy.

sources.originalTitle: EA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereft

segments.body: The writer recalls struggling with Mass Effect at first, then becoming absorbed by its characters and the choices that shaped the trilogy’s story. Decisions carried forward across the games, making the player feel responsible for the lives and fate of the crew.

segments.title: A studio’s legacy
segments.body: The article says EA announced BioWare’s closure, cancellation of its next Mass Effect game and more than 400 job losses. The writer argues that, despite the studio’s recent failures, its role-playing games helped define the genre and that the cancellation leaves fans without a hoped-for continuation.

content.headline: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort makes family gaming feel like a holiday
content.shortHeadline: Switch Sports Resort brings the family back together
content.standfirst: Nintendo’s sequel adds new sports, island exploration and customisable characters to the accessible Wii Sports formula. The review finds it easy to enjoy together and deep enough to keep a keen child playing.

image.caption: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort.

sources.originalTitle: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort review – Wii Sports lives on in this effortlessly appealing collection of games

segments.body: Switch Sports Resort brings back tennis, bowling and volleyball, adds golf and basketball, and introduces activities including archery, skateboarding and thumb wrestling. The reviewer finds the games simple to pick up, with the deliberately silly touches helping make them fun across ages.

segments.title: An island to explore
segments.body: Jetski and plane activities let players travel around the resort, while outfits, leagues and variations such as bowling obstacle courses add reasons to return. After a week of play, the reviewer expects it to remain a family fixture.

content.headline: Penguin Colony turns an Antarctic expedition into a strange, absorbing game
content.shortHeadline: Penguin Colony finds wonder in a frozen wasteland
content.standfirst: This exploration game casts players as penguins navigating an Antarctic world of Nazis, Lovecraftian horror and scattered words. The review finds it technically uneven but strikingly original in its treatment of history and discovery.

image.caption: A penguin in the Antarctic world of Penguin Colony.

sources.originalTitle: Penguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors

segments.body: Players guide penguins across Antarctica, switching between birds with different abilities and collecting words rather than conventional treasure. The journey begins among human remnants, then leads into stranger spaces as a narrator recounts an earlier expedition.

segments.title: A different way to see
segments.body: The game layers its penguin exploration with Nazi characters, Lovecraftian imagery and unsettling archival material. The review reports some audio and control glitches, but praises the game’s final invitation to explore beyond the obvious route and find a larger world.

content.headline: Rainbow Six Tactics turns Ubisoft Paris from Mario to military strategy
content.shortHeadline: How Ubisoft Paris made Rainbow Six Tactics
content.standfirst: The studio behind Mario + Rabbids has shifted to a turn-based Rainbow Six spin-off. Its developers explain how the game translates the shooter’s planning and teamwork into a slower tactical format.

image.caption: An illustration for Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics.

sources.originalTitle: From Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics

segments.body: Rainbow Six Tactics replaces Mario + Rabbids’ bright fantasy with a military setting built around surveillance, planning and coordinated attacks. In a demonstration, a four-person unit uses drones, explosives and a pincer move to breach a warehouse.

segments.title: Planning with freedom
segments.body: Creative director Elie Benhamou says the series’ emphasis on preparation and consequences suits turn-based strategy. Developers describe a game with 15 operators and several possible approaches to missions, while acknowledging that realistic settings require close collaboration between artists and level designers.

content.headline: Lara Croft at 30: the marketing and design choices that misread her
content.shortHeadline: Lara Croft’s biggest missteps at 30
content.standfirst: A celebratory anniversary feature revisits the Tomb Raider icon’s less successful games, advertising and screen portrayals. Its argument is that Lara’s appeal has repeatedly been mistaken for a reason to sexualise or diminish her.

image.caption: Lara Croft in Tomb Raider IV–VI Remastered.

sources.originalTitle: Lara Croft is 30! We look at the video game icon’s biggest blunders

segments.body: Thirty years after her first appearance, Lara Croft has become one of gaming’s most recognisable characters. The retrospective recalls the rapid annual release schedule imposed on the original developers and the disappointing Tomb Raider: Chronicles and Angel of Darkness.

segments.title: A character misunderstood
segments.body: The article criticises years of advertising that reduced Lara to a marketing prop, as well as later creative decisions that put her in the role of a damsel in distress. It argues that her lasting appeal lies in her independence and the strength of the original games.

content.headline: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 review: a spectacular, crowded campaign
content.shortHeadline: Modern Warfare 4 is a thrilling action-game ride
content.standfirst: The new Call of Duty campaign moves from rooftop parkour to a battle at a North Korean airbase, while multiplayer and extraction modes add more to play. The review praises its polish but questions whether its military fantasy will attract a wider audience.

image.caption: A scene from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

sources.originalTitle: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 review – a thrilling airport novel of a game

segments.body: Modern Warfare 4’s six-hour campaign mixes set pieces, including rooftop parkour and a Paris car chase, with an open-world section and ethically difficult moments. The review calls it a breathless, entertaining ride, though it finds Captain Price’s story underdeveloped near the end.

segments.title: More than the campaign
segments.body: Multiplayer refines the series’ fast movement, while the reworked DMZ extraction mode offers missions, upgrades and encounters with other players. The reviewer says the package is polished and expansive, but notes that its gung-ho military fantasy may limit its appeal as major competition approaches.

content.headline: Modern Warfare 4’s developers put character alongside the spectacle
content.shortHeadline: How Modern Warfare 4 built a story around its battles
content.standfirst: Infinity Ward’s narrative director describes how the campaign’s Korean setting, split storylines and quieter scenes were developed alongside its action. The feature explains the studio’s aim to make players feel connected to the characters caught up in the conflict.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 combines large battles with a story about those caught in the conflict.

sources.originalTitle: ‘The audience gets to be in on it’: How narrative-led gameplay is Call of Duty’s greatest weapon

segments.body: Modern Warfare 4 follows a South Korean conscript caught in an invasion and John Price on a separate mission. Narrative director Jeff Negus says the team aimed to make the conflict feel grounded, consult people with military and Korean language experience, and avoid repeating earlier stories.

segments.title: Making action matter
segments.body: Negus describes a process in which story and gameplay were developed together, so that action would mean more when players knew the people involved. The article also notes that quieter character scenes and the story’s family tensions provide a human counterweight to its large-scale battles.

content.headline: Personalised mRNA vaccine cuts melanoma recurrence risk in phase III trial
content.shortHeadline: Personalised vaccine cuts melanoma recurrence risk in trial
content.standfirst: In a large trial, adding a bespoke mRNA vaccine to immunotherapy reduced the two-year risk of melanoma recurrence or death. The treatment is not yet approved, and its longer-term benefit remains unknown.

image.caption: Prof Georgina Long, medical director of the Melanoma Institute Australia.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Bespoke’ mRNA vaccine significantly reduces risk of melanoma recurrence or death, clinical trial shows

segments.body: The Australian-led phase III trial involved 1,137 people whose melanoma had been surgically removed but was at high risk of returning. After two years, 82% of those given the personalised vaccine intismeran alongside pembrolizumab were alive and recurrence-free, compared with 70% receiving pembrolizumab alone. The combination reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 42%.

segments.title: What remains to be learned
segments.body: The vaccine is tailored to mutations in each person’s tumour, targeting up to 34 mutations. Researchers describe the findings as a significant advance, but the trial does not establish whether the combination improves long-term survival. Some patients may not respond, and further study and regulatory review are needed before it could become standard treatment.

content.headline: Scientists recreate the colour-changing effect of a Roman glass cup
content.shortHeadline: Scientists recreate a Roman cup’s colour-changing glass
content.standfirst: A Sheffield team has reproduced the striking green-to-red optical effect of the 1,600-year-old Lycurgus Cup. The work offers a closer match to its colours and clues to the demanding craft behind them.

image.caption: The Lycurgus Cup appears green in ordinary light and red when lit from behind.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s magic’: scientists rediscover how to make ancient Roman colour-changing glass

segments.body: The Lycurgus Cup appears jade green in ordinary light and ruby red when lit from behind. Scientists at the University of Sheffield have replicated the effect using an ancient recipe derived from a fragment of Roman dichroic glass, embedding tiny gold and silver particles in molten glass as it cooled.

segments.title: A difficult craft
segments.body: The nanoparticles interact with light in different ways: they block some colours as light passes through the glass, while scattering light reflected from its surface. Archaeological materials expert Ian Freestone said the Sheffield version is more precise than a similar-coloured glass made in the 1960s. He said the colour’s sensitivity to furnace conditions suggests Roman makers may have found it difficult to control.

content.headline: Biodiversity fund for drug companies has received just $7,085
content.shortHeadline: Biodiversity fund has received only $7,085 from industry
content.standfirst: The Cali Fund was designed to channel money from businesses using genetic information from nature into conservation, but its coffers remain almost empty. Pharmaceutical companies question how the voluntary mechanism is designed.

image.caption: Researchers collect samples from nature for genetic sequencing.

sources.originalTitle: Big pharma accused of ‘free-riding on nature’ as global fund attracts just $7,000

segments.body: The Cali Fund aims to raise $1bn a year for conservation, with at least half directed to priorities identified by Indigenous peoples and local communities. More than 18 months after its launch, it had received $10,656 in commitments, with $7,085 deposited, according to figures reported at the start of the Cop17 biodiversity summit in Armenia.

segments.title: Dispute over contributions
segments.body: A Zero Carbon Analytics analysis estimated that the 15 largest pharmaceutical companies could have contributed $756m under the fund’s voluntary guidelines, based on their previous year’s performance. The industry says the mechanism’s design is problematic: it argues that not all medicines rely on digital genetic information and that the fund may overlap with existing laws. The fund’s spokesperson said contributions may remain modest while its operating systems are completed.

content.headline: UK flu season has started early, but that does not mean it will be severe
content.shortHeadline: Early flu season does not necessarily mean a worse one
content.standfirst: Flu infections are rising earlier than usual in the UK, prompting health officials to urge eligible people to get vaccinated. Experts say the timing alone cannot predict how severe the season will be.

image.caption: Respiratory viruses are circulating earlier than usual in the UK.

sources.originalTitle: Why so many people are sick right now

segments.body: UK flu activity is rising earlier than usual, although rates were still relatively low when the report was published. Possible explanations include changes in circulating flu strains and the timing of the southern hemisphere season, which can influence which strains reach the UK. Scientists are still debating why respiratory viruses peak when they do.

segments.title: What an early start tells us
